{{Short description|Partially ordered set}}
In [[order theory]], a '''continuous poset''' is a [[partially ordered set]] in which every element is the [[directed set|directed]] [[supremum]] of elements approximating it.

== Definitions ==
Let <math>a,b\in P</math> be two elements of a [[preordered set]] <math>(P,\lesssim)</math>. Then we say that <math>a</math> '''approximates''' <math>b</math>, or that <math>a</math> is '''way-below''' <math>b</math>, if the following two equivalent conditions are satisfied.
* For any [[directed set]] <math>D\subseteq P</math> such that <math>b\lesssim\sup D</math>, there is a <math>d\in D</math> such that <math>a\lesssim d</math>.
* For any [[ideal (order theory)|ideal]] <math>I\subseteq P</math> such that <math>b\lesssim\sup I</math>, <math>a\in I</math>.
If <math>a</math> approximates <math>b</math>, we write <math>a\ll b</math>. The approximation relation <math>\ll</math> is a [[transitive relation]] that is weaker than the original order, also [[antisymmetric relation|antisymmetric]] if <math>P</math> is a [[partially ordered set]], but not necessarily a [[preorder]]. It is a preorder if and only if <math>(P,\lesssim)</math> satisfies the [[ascending chain condition]].<ref name="Gierz">{{cite book|author-link6=Dana Scott|date=2003|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511542725|first1=Gerhard|first2=Karl|first3=Klaus|first4=Jimmie|first5=Michael|first6=Dana S.|isbn=978-0-521-80338-0|language=en|last1=Gierz|last2=Hofmann|last3=Keimel|last4=Lawson|last5=Mislove|last6=Scott|location=Cambridge|mr=1975381|publisher=Cambridge University Press|series=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and Its Applications|title=Continuous lattices and domains|volume=93|zbl=1088.06001}}</ref>{{rp|p.52, Examples I-1.3, (4)}}

For any <math>a\in P</math>, let
:<math>\mathop\Uparrow a=\{b\in L\mid a\ll b\}</math>
:<math>\mathop\Downarrow a=\{b\in L\mid b\ll a\}</math>
Then <math>\mathop\Uparrow a</math> is an [[upper set]], and <math>\mathop\Downarrow a</math> a [[lower set]]. If <math>P</math> is an [[upper-semilattice]], <math>\mathop\Downarrow a</math> is a [[directed set]] (that is, <math>b,c\ll a</math> implies <math>b\vee c\ll a</math>), and therefore an [[ideal (order theory)|ideal]].

A [[preordered set]] <math>(P,\lesssim)</math> is called a '''continuous preordered set''' if for any <math>a\in P</math>, the subset <math>\mathop\Downarrow a</math> is [[directed set|directed]] and <math>a=\sup\mathop\Downarrow a</math>.

== Properties ==
=== The interpolation property ===
For any two elements <math>a,b\in P</math> of a continuous preordered set <math>(P,\lesssim)</math>, <math>a\ll b</math> if and only if for any [[directed set]] <math>D\subseteq P</math> such that <math>b\lesssim\sup D</math>, there is a <math>d\in D</math> such that <math>a\ll d</math>. From this follows the interpolation property of the continuous preordered set <math>(P,\lesssim)</math>: for any <math>a,b\in P</math> such that <math>a\ll b</math> there is a <math>c\in P</math> such that <math>a\ll c\ll b</math>.

=== Continuous dcpos ===
For any two elements <math>a,b\in P</math> of a continuous [[directed-complete partially ordered set|dcpo]] <math>(P,\le)</math>, the following two conditions are equivalent.<ref name="Gierz" />{{rp|p.61, Proposition I-1.19(i)}}
* <math>a\ll b</math> and <math>a\ne b</math>.
* For any [[directed set]] <math>D\subseteq P</math> such that <math>b\le\sup D</math>, there is a <math>d\in D</math> such that <math>a\ll d</math> and <math>a\ne d</math>.
Using this it can be shown that the following stronger interpolation property is true for continuous dcpos. For any <math>a,b\in P</math> such that <math>a\ll b</math> and <math>a\ne b</math>, there is a <math>c\in P</math> such that <math>a\ll c\ll b</math> and <math>a\ne c</math>.<ref name="Gierz" />{{rp|p.61, Proposition I-1.19(ii)}}

For a [[directed-complete partially ordered set|dcpo]] <math>(P,\le)</math>, the following conditions are equivalent.<ref name="Gierz" />{{rp|Theorem I-1.10}}
* <math>P</math> is continuous.
* The [[supremum]] map <math>\sup \colon \operatorname{Ideal}(P)\to P</math> from the [[partially ordered set]] of [[ideal (order theory)|ideal]]s of <math>P</math> to <math>P</math> has a [[left adjoint]].
In this case, the actual left adjoint is
:<math>{\Downarrow} \colon P\to\operatorname{Ideal}(P)</math>
:<math>\mathord\Downarrow\dashv\sup</math>

=== Continuous complete lattices ===
For any two elements <math>a,b\in L</math> of a [[complete lattice]] <math>L</math>, <math>a\ll b</math> if and only if for any subset <math>A\subseteq L</math> such that <math>b\le\sup A</math>, there is a [[finite subset]] <math>F\subseteq A</math> such that <math>a\le\sup F</math>.

Let <math>L</math> be a [[complete lattice]]. Then the following conditions are equivalent.
* <math>L</math> is continuous.
* The [[supremum]] map <math>\sup \colon \operatorname{Ideal}(L)\to L</math> from the [[complete lattice]] of [[ideal (order theory)|ideal]]s of <math>L</math> to <math>L</math> preserves arbitrary [[infima]].
* For any family <math>\mathcal D</math> of [[directed set]]s of <math>L</math>, <math>\textstyle\inf_{D\in\mathcal D}\sup D=\sup_{f\in\prod\mathcal D}\inf_{D\in\mathcal D}f(D)</math>.
* <math>L</math> is [[isomorphic]] to the [[image (mathematics)|image]] of a [[Scott-continuous]] [[idempotent map]] <math>r \colon \{0,1\}^\kappa\to\{0,1\}^\kappa</math> on the [[direct product|direct power]] of arbitrarily many two-point lattices <math>\{0,1\}</math>.<ref name="Grätzer">{{cite book|date=2011|doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-0018-1|first=George|isbn=978-3-0348-0017-4|language=en|last=Grätzer|authorlink = George Grätzer|lccn=2011921250|location=Basel|mr=2768581|publisher=Springer|title=Lattice Theory: Foundation|zbl=1233.06001}}</ref>{{rp|p.56, Theorem 44}}

A continuous [[complete lattice]] is often called a '''continuous lattice'''.

== Examples ==
=== Lattices of open sets ===
For a [[topological space]] <math>X</math>, the following conditions are equivalent.
* The [[complete Heyting algebra]] <math>\operatorname{Open}(X)</math> of open sets of <math>X</math> is a continuous [[complete Heyting algebra]].
* The [[sobrification]] of <math>X</math> is a [[locally compact space]] (in the sense that every point has a [[compact set|compact]] [[local base]])
* <math>X</math> is an [[exponentiable object]] in the category <math>\operatorname{Top}</math> of [[topological space]]s.<ref name="Gierz" />{{rp|p.196, Theorem II-4.12}} That is, the [[functor]] <math>(-)\times X\colon\operatorname{Top}\to\operatorname{Top}</math> has a [[right adjoint]].
